title: FluentValidation
description: FluentValidation is a library for building strongly typed validation rules using a fluent interface. It keeps validation logic separate from your models and provides a clean alternative to DataAnnotations.

data.text: FluentValidation lets you define validation rules in separate validator classes instead of decorating your models with attributes. This keeps your domain models clean and makes complex validation logic easier to read and test.

data.title: Defining a Validator
data.content: Create a validator for a CreateUserCommand.

terms.definition: A class that inherits from AbstractValidator<T> and defines validation rules for a specific type.
Starts a fluent rule chain for a specific property.
Sets a custom error message for a failed validation rule.

data.title: ASP.NET Core Integration
data.text: Use FluentValidation.AspNetCore to automatically replace DataAnnotations with FluentValidation in MVC and Web API controllers.

FluentValidation builds a validator class with a fluent rule chain. Rules can be async — checking uniqueness against the database — and can be composed from child validators. In ASP.NET Core a single `AddFluentValidationAutoValidation` call replaces the automatic DataAnnotations validation.

data.title: A validator with an async uniqueness rule
Interview angle: validation is not authorization
data.text: Validation checks that input is well-formed; authorization checks whether the caller may perform the action at all. They run at different stages and a request can pass one and fail the other. Also, never trust client-side validation: the server-side validator is the one that matters, and both can share the same rules if the client is written in the same language.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Rules are expressed with a readable fluent API
It integrates cleanly with ASP.NET Core pipelines
data.takeaway: FluentValidation scales better than DataAnnotations for complex business rules.

data.title: Exercise: Validate an Order
data.description: Create a validator for an Order class with multiple rules.
steps: Create an Order class with OrderId, CustomerEmail, Amount, and OrderDate properties
Create an OrderValidator inheriting from AbstractValidator<Order>
Add rules: OrderId > 0, valid email, Amount > 0, OrderDate cannot be in the past
Write a small console app that validates an order and prints any failures
data.expectedOutcome: Invalid orders produce descriptive validation errors; valid orders pass all rules.
